title: Phase-accumulating hyperfine strain sensing with rare-earth-ion phase memories
abstract: Long-lived hyperfine coherences in rare-earth-ion crystals provide controlled phase evolution windows for metrology. We use this resource to propose an experimental protocol for accessing strain shifts of ground state hyperfine transitions in non-Kramers rare-earth-ion doped (REID) materials, a quantity that is difficult to access directly with conventional spectroscopic methods. Starting from the crystal field Hamiltonian, we relate the response to strain-dependent effective quadrupole and Zeeman tensors, including changes in electronic wave functions, virtual electronic admixtures, and the bare nuclear quadrupole interaction. The protocol optically prepares a selected hyperfine class, uses a phase-controlled rf $π/2$ pulse to create the sensing coherence, and applies synchronized dynamical decoupling pulses during the phase evolution interval so that a coherent ac strain drive accumulates phase rather than averaging away. The accumulated phase is then retrieved by Raman heterodyne readout. The resulting framework provides a route to understanding strain-induced hyperfine couplings in non-Kramers REID systems.
summary: This paper outlines an advanced quantum sensing protocol to measure strain effects on hyperfine transitions in rare-earth-ion crystals. It uses long-lived hyperfine coherence, enhanced by dynamical decoupling pulses, to accumulate a phase proportional to the applied strain. The method is theoretically derived and compared against other quantum memory readout techniques, providing a route to understanding strain-induced couplings in solid-state quantum systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of developing a sensitive method to measure strain-induced shifts in the ground state hyperfine transitions of rare-earth-ion-doped (REID) crystals, a measurement difficult via conventional spectroscopy.
main_result: A protocol is proposed that uses phase-accumulating hyperfine coherence, enhanced by synchronized dynamical decoupling pulses, to measure the strain-dependent hyperfine coupling coefficient ($G_s$).
method: The method involves optically preparing a hyperfine state, creating a transverse coherence via an rf $\pi/2$ pulse, allowing the coherence to evolve under an oscillating strain field, and finally reading out the accumulated phase using Raman heterodyne detection.
model_or_system: The system is based on rare-earth ions (e.g., Pr$^{3+}$) in crystals, modeled using a Hamiltonian incorporating crystal field, hyperfine, Zeeman, and strain terms. The strain dependence is derived by expanding effective quadrupole and Zeeman tensors around an operating point.
key_observables: The primary observable is the accumulated phase ($\Phi_{\epsilon}$), which is proportional to the strain ($\epsilon_a$) via the measurable strain coefficient ($G_s$).
important_parameters: The protocol utilizes dynamical decoupling (DD) pulses to ensure the accumulated phase grows linearly with time under AC strain, and the measurement is optimized near a Zero-First-Order-Zeeman (ZEFOZ) point.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability to perform a differential measurement to isolate the strain phase, and comparisons between readout schemes rely on specific scaling laws and approximations regarding coherence amplitude.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the entire measurement sequence: optical pumping, rf $\pi/2$ write pulse, the storage interval with DD pulses and AC strain, and the final optical read field generating the Raman sideband.
paper_structure: The paper moves from defining the physical problem and Hamiltonian to detailing the experimental protocol (preparation, evolution, readout). It then provides theoretical derivations for the strain coupling tensors and compares the sensitivity limits of the proposed RF-write/Raman-read scheme against alternative optical memory techniques.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics and quantum optics as it details a sophisticated quantum sensing protocol that leverages long-lived coherence in solid-state systems, combining concepts from quantum memory, dynamical decoupling, and high-precision spectroscopy.
